lesson.title: Boots, Trees, and Paychecks: FDR's Tree Army
lesson.summary: The Civilian Conservation Corps put unemployed young men to work planting trees, building trails, and fighting erosion, sending most of their pay home to families struggling through the Depression.
lesson.body:
By early 1933, the Great Depression had left roughly a quarter of American workers unemployed, and young men without jobs or prospects worried policymakers as much as the economic numbers themselves. Franklin Roosevelt believed putting these men to useful outdoor work would relieve family hardship while also repairing forests, soils, and parks that decades of unmanaged logging, farming, and drought had damaged.

Within weeks of taking office, Roosevelt pushed the Emergency Conservation Work Act through Congress, signing it on March 31, 1933. It created the Civilian Conservation Corps, which enrolled unmarried young men, originally ages 18 to 25, in work camps run day to day by the Army but focused entirely on conservation labor rather than military training. Over the program's life, CCC crews planted an estimated 3 billion trees, built trails, roads, and lodges still used in national and state parks today, and worked to control soil erosion and wildfires.

The pay structure made clear this was family relief as much as youth employment. Enrollees earned about 30 dollars a month, and the government required that 25 of those dollars be sent directly home to their families, turning each enrollee's labor into a steady household income at a time when steady income of any kind was scarce.

The program was not free of the era's inequalities. Camps in the South were generally segregated by race, and a separate Indian Division, organized under Bureau of Indian Affairs commissioner John Collier, ran conservation work on tribal lands. Even with these limits, the CCC became one of the most popular of Roosevelt's New Deal programs, remembered fondly by many who served in it.

As war mobilization began pulling young men into defense industries and eventually the military itself, the need for the CCC's labor pool faded, and Congress let the program end in 1942. It remains a clear example of the broader New Deal strategy: using direct federal employment to address both an economic emergency and a longer term public need.
